title: ‘Wildwood’ Director Travis Knight Reflects on Animated Feature’s 16-Year Journey at London Premiere: ‘When We Started This, Barack Obama Was a Fresh-Faced President’
description: Stop-motion animation is a notoriously time-consuming method to make a film, with most features taking several years of painstakingly detailed work
body:
Stop-motion animation is a notoriously time-consuming method to make a film, with most features taking several years of painstakingly detailed work by vast teams of creatives. 

	But few have likely taken as long as Laika‘s sweeping fantasy epic “Wildwood,” which had its world premiere at the BFI London Film Festival on Sunday. 

	Speaking on stage at the premiere alongside voice stars Carey Mulligan, Peyton Elizabeth Lee and Jacob Tremblay, director Travis Knight explained the stop-motion process to the audience at the Royal Festival Hall.
	

	“Basically we build thousands and thousands of this tiny little objects, we put them in front of a camera and set lights  and we take a picture, we move them a microscopic distance, we take another picture, we move them another microscopic distance, we take another picture,” he said.  “And we repeat that process over and over until either the film emerges or society collapses.”


	On “Wildwood,” — which Knight had previously acknowledged was the most ambitious Laika had ever attempted — production started in 2021 in the midst of COVID, but the development had actually begun some 10 years earlier, when Laika optioned the book by Colin Meloy and Carson Ellis. 

	“This movie took us 16 years to make,” Knight explains. When we started Barack Obama was a fresh-faced  president in his very first term. I could have become a medical doctor twice in the time it took us to make this movie. A child who was born when we started this could have driven me to the premiere.”

	Following its world premiere at the London Film Festival, which runs until Oct. 17, “Laika” is due to be released on Oct. 23 by Fathom Entertainment in the U.S. and by Black Bear in the U.K. The film marks the first by Laika to receive a PG-13 rating.

schema.headline: ‘Wildwood’ Director Travis Knight Reflects on Animated Feature’s 16-Year Journey at London Premiere: ‘When We Started This, Barack Obama Was a Fresh-Faced President’

title: Spain Hits Mipcom With Prestige Dramas, Reality Formats, Headed by Can Yaman, ‘Nowhere’ Star Anna Castillo and ‘La Mesias’ Lead Carmen Machi
description: AdriftBuendía Estudios Canarias, Boomerang TV, AtresmediaFive fishermen, who are presumed dead, return home two years later, upending the lives thei
body:
AdriftBuendía Estudios Canarias, Boomerang TV, AtresmediaFive fishermen, who are presumed dead, return home two years later, upending the lives their wives had rebuilt without them. Paula Echevarría (“Velvet”) leads the ensemble in this 10-episode drama, co-written by Susana López Rubio (“The Time in Between”).

	The Big DateIncís TV, 3CatCan AI find your perfect match? A hundred singles test the theory in this Catalan dating format hosted by Dulceida. After 1.5 million-plus digital views on 3Cat, BBC Studios snapped up international adaptation rights.
	

	The Butterfly LabyrinthSecuoya StudiosCan Yaman (“Daydreamer”) plays a betrayed secret agent who is branded Spain’s most wanted man. Shot entirely in Spain and in Spanish, the espionage thriller gives Secuoya Studios a star-driven international project.


	Bumpy, the BearKrakatoa, Spiritum Entertainment, RTVEA playful bear turns everyday discoveries into musical learning adventures. The preschool IP spans 52 shorts and 52 music videos in Spanish, English and Portuguese, extending across TV, music, publishing, toys and licensing.

	CaldasCaldas La Serie, Secuoya Studios, Disney+Domingo Villar’s bestseller “The Last Boat” becomes a crime series with Javier Gutiérrez (“Marshland”) as Vigo-based inspector Leo Caldas and Hovik Keuchkerian (“The Platform 2”) as his volatile new partner.

	The CastleMovistar Plus, Caballo Films, Mafalda EntertainmentOver the years, a Spanish police unit works to bring down an ambitious prostitution kingpin. The series, co-created by Isabel Peña, Rodrigo Sorogoyen‘s regular co-scribe, it was a big hit at September’s San Sebastián Film Festival.
	

	Celeste, Season 2Movistar Plus, the Mediapro StudioWinner of Series Mania’s Panorama best series, as well as actress kudos for Carmen Machi (“La Mesías”), who brings a moving humanity to her role of a dowdy, lonely tax inspector. Created by Diego San José (“Jakarta”).

	Dating in Barcelona, Season 3Arca, FilmaxBarcelona’s dating scene returns with International Emmy-winning “I, Addict” star Oriol Pla alongside Emma Vilarasau and Anna Castillo (“Nowhere”). Earlier seasons led TV3 primetime and played Prime Video Spain.

	Death in LlanesK 2000, 100 Balas A real-life councillor’s murder fuels this SkyShowtime crime drama, where political rivalries and an unexpected love triangle drive the mystery. Gerardo Olivares directs.

	Forever HomeFilmNation Entertainment, the Mediapro StudioA corpse beneath an idyllic home detonates this domestic thriller adapted from Graham Norton’s bestseller. Amy Nuttall (“Downton Abbey”) and Douglas Henshall (“Shetland”) star; Imagina Sales launches international sales at Mipcom.

	Gènesi3Cat, Minoria Absoluta, Fishcorb MediaFerran Adrià’s transformation of his eatery El Bulli into a global culinary phenomenon gets the prestige-drama treatment. Miquel Fernández plays Adrià, while New Regency launches international sales at Mipcom; Netflix is already on board for major territories.

	Hidden BrushstrokesBuendía Estudios Canarias, AtresmediaFrom the writers of “Ángela” comes a domestic noir about a marriage built on lies. A marriage starts to implode when a wife, (Toni Acosta, “Phenomena”) spots her pilot husband, (Rodolfo Sancho, “The Department of Time”), in Tenerife when he claims to be abroad.

	InfamyEvafilms, HBO MaxA 20-year-old disappearance haunts this six-episode thriller, with Susana Abaitua (“A Ghost in the Battle”) as a lawyer obsessed with two missing girls in a remote Basque community. Based on Ledicia Costas’ novel.

	Killing a BearMovistar Plus, Arte FranceIn 2020, Cachou, a brown bear, is found dead in a ravine, sparking a criminal investigation. Fact-based series probes ancestral Spain’s battle with new global forces, say creators Jorge and Alberto Sánchez-Cabezudo (“The Zone”).

	Many People Need to DieMovistar Plus, Corte y Confección de PelículasMovistar Plus’ most-watched series of 2026, it turns on three thirtysomething women friends, depicting Millennial angst with scathing realism and LOL humor. It also marks the consecration of creator/writer Victoria Martín as a major comedic voice in Spain.
	

	Marusía: Naval AcademyUnicorn Content, Mediaset EspañaA cadet’s mysterious death greets the first woman to head Spain’s Naval Academy. Lucía Jiménez (“When No One Sees Us”) stars in the Galicia-shot drama, mixing mystery with coming-of-age tensions.

	OliviaStudio60, Womack Studios, Disney+A celebrity TV weatherman retreats with his daughter to his estranged father’s olive groves, reopening old wounds. Pablo Chiapella (“La Que se Avecina”) stars in Juanma Pachón’s (“Welcome to Eden”) comedy-drama about family, roots and second chances.

	Red on WhiteGood Mood (Mediawan), RTVE“Red Eagle” creator Daniel Écija mixes crime, romance and comedy in a procedural built around forensic linguistics. Hugo Silva (“The Cook of Castamar”) plays a troubled detective opposite María Hervás (“The Immortal”).

	RocíoRTVE, Movistar Plus, Boomerang TVMusic legend Rocío Jurado gets a bio series charting her rise from Andalusian village Chipiona to international stardom. “The Secret of Puente Viejo” creator Aurora Guerra writes; the four-parter shot across 66-plus locations with nearly 2,000 extras.

	She, Damned SoulMediaset España, Plano a PlanoA forbidden romance drives this Manuel Rivas adaptation as a charismatic priest falls for his cousin’s wife. Maxi Iglesias (“Valeria”), Karina Kolokolchykova (“The Grandmother”) and Martiño Rivas (“The Boarding School”) star.

	Sons of the ApocalypseDeep Com RootsFormer Jehovah’s Witness Becky leaves her closed religious community and travels from Spain to New York after falling for an outsider to her religion. The three-episode docuseries premiered on Movistar Plus.

	Traffic Jam, Season 4Onza, Prime VideoAnother monumental traffic jam traps a fresh cast including Raúl Cimas (“Muchachada Nui”), Pepe Viyuela (“Aída”) and Marta Hazas (“Velvet”). Already reupped for Season 5.

	UCO: The Key HoursOnza, Prime VideoA TV crew embeds with an elite Spanish Guardia Civil investigative unit, accessing real operations involving money laundering, smuggling, violent crime and fugitives. “A History of the Future” director Ferran Estellés helms the factual series.

title: John Malkovich Says the Oscars Race Was a ‘Different World’ When He Was Last on the Campaign Trail: ‘Now, That’s the Only Way to Get People to Go to Theaters’
description: John Malkovich has been highly tipped for an Oscar nomination for his performance in Martin McDonagh’s CIA black comedy “Wild Horse Nine,” making it
body:
John Malkovich has been highly tipped for an Oscar nomination for his performance in Martin McDonagh’s CIA black comedy “Wild Horse Nine,” making it his first real shot at an Academy Award in three decades. The 72-year-old actor was previously nominated for best supporting actor in “Places in the Heart” (1984) and “In the Line of Fire” (1993), but never won.

	Speaking at a London Film Festival Screen Talk on Sunday, Malkovich said he views awards buzz “probably differently than I did then, because the movie business existed.” 
	

	“It maintained an — undeserved, in my opinion, but nevertheless — a very, very high position in the culture. And when I say ‘undeserved,’ meaning there weren’t that many ‘Chinatowns’ or ‘Godfathers’ or ‘Godfathers II,'” Malkovich said. “So now, that’s the only way to get people to go to the theaters, the whole thing. And that’s months and months and months.”


	Reflecting on the last time he was up for an Oscar over 30 years ago, Malkovich said the campaigning was not so intense. “When I was nominated for an Academy Award, someone said, ‘You’re nominated for an Academy Award,'” he said.

	However, Malkovich has never been a huge fan of awards ceremonies anyway, and only attended the Oscars once, when he was nominated for “Places in the Heart.” He told the London crowd that he felt quite overwhelmed by the experience. 

	“I had a manager called Phyllis Carlyle, and we were on our way to the Dorothy Chandler Pavilion, and she was a little bit… bossy. She said, ‘Now honey, when we get there, there’s gonna be a lot of people,'” he recalled. “And I said, ‘OK, but we can just go in a side door, right?’ And she, right in my face, goes ‘Honey! It’s the Oscars, there’s no side door!’ So, I mean, that’s kind of my native personality in the face of that kind of onslaught.”
	

	Malkovich acknowledged that Hollywood as a whole has changed quite a lot since the last time he was on the awards trail, with the advent of streaming taking over theaters. Often, he said, campaigning for a film is the only way to make the public go see it in theaters.

	“Both ‘The Killing Fields,’ which was a 1984 Oscars film I think, and ‘Places in the Heart,’ they’re already been out, they’d already made their money, they were already successful. The same with ‘In the Line of Fire,'” he said. “It was really a different world. Now, that kind of seems to be the only way to get people to actually go to a theater.” 

	He isn’t too bothered by it, though. “I’m 72 years old, things change,” he said. “I don’t really like thinking things aren’t what they used to be. They just change, and you either change with them or die. And I prefer to change with them. I’ll die, anyway.”

	“Wild Horse Nine,” in which he stars opposite Sam Rockwell as a veteran CIA agent, held its U.K. premiere at London Film Festival on Friday. Set shortly before the 1973 Chilean coup d’etat, the two are dispatched to Easter Island, where they must confront both their dark pasts and present conspiracies.

	“Wild Horse Nine” first premiered at Venice Film Festival in September, where it received rave reviews and Malkovich took home the best actor prize. At a Venice press conference, Malkovich humbly shrugged off the praise, saying: “That is incredibly kind. I’ve had a long career, and I’ve had spectacular collaborations with writers, directors and actors. I never feel in competition with any of them. For me, it’s a very nice thing. But the nicest thing is the film getting attention. And the film has several terrific performers, and it’s beautifully written and directed. That’s what matters to me.”

schema.headline: John Malkovich Says the Oscars Race Was a ‘Different World’ When He Was Last on the Campaign Trail: ‘Now, That’s the Only Way to Get People to Go to Theaters’

title: Javier Bardem on Adding Homoeroticism to 007 and Telling Sam Mendes That His ‘Skyfall’ Villain Should Be Someone Who ‘Wants to Have Sex With Bond’
description: Javier Bardem‘s “Skyfall” villain Raoul Silva is widely considered to be one of the best James Bond baddies across the entire franchise, a sadistic
body:
Javier Bardem‘s “Skyfall” villain Raoul Silva is widely considered to be one of the best James Bond baddies across the entire franchise, a sadistic and flirtatious cyber-terrorist with bleached-blond locks who gave 007 arguably his most homoerotic scene to date. 

	“We are the last two rats. We can either eat each other, or eat everyone else,” Silva says as he unbuttons the shirt of Daniel Craig’s Bond, tied to a chair. He then moves his hands down Bond’s thighs, offering “Well, there’s a first time for everything” (to which Bond famously replies “What makes you think this is my first time?”)
	

	As it happens, it was Bardem himself who wanted to dial up the sexuality of his character, and found a willing director in Sam Mendes. 


	“We went through the reading of it and [Mendes] was so open to what I was proposing to do with the sexuality of the character,” Bardem revealed at a special Screen Talk at the BFI London Film Festival on Sunday. “Because I said, ‘Listen, all the villains have done everything to destroy the world, but what about something person? What about something like, besides destroying the world, he wants to have sex with Bond.'”

	According to Bardem, Mendes’ first response was was “‘Let me talk to the studio’… and the studio was very brave!” The scene, he noted was one that “now lasts in the memory of the audience” because it “put Bond out of his place in a moment with a situation that he’s not been to before — and the way he comes out of it is brilliant.”

	Bardem also revealed that in the prison cell scene in “Skyfall” with Craig (who he said was “adorable”) and Judi Dench as M (“what a gift!”), he was so overcome that he forgot his lines.
	

	“Sam said action and then [Dench] comes in and nobody talks… I forgot the lines!,” he said, to which Mendes asked him what was going on. “I’m sorry, I just realized that I’m in a James Bond movie. Excuse me, I just saw Judi Dench as M and James Bond looking at me and thought ‘Fuck, I’m in a James Bond movie!’ Sorry, let’s do it again!”

	Across a wide-ranging conversation about his career and craft, Bardem — the first Spanish actor to win the best actor Oscar (for “No Country for Old Men”), holder of a record 5 Goya leading actor awards and one of a select group to have won Venice’s Volpi Cup twice — discussed a selection of his more than 65 screens credits and collaborations with numerous filmmakers. But he even went as far back as his first brush with acting as a five year old in the 1974 Spanish TV series “El Picaro,” which starred his mother, the late actress Pilar Bardem.

	“My mother was in the show and this kid got sick and she said, ‘Don’t worry. I have my my kid,'” he revealed. In the scene, he said he started to cry. “And [the director] said ‘I love it, I love it, he’s a dramatic actor!’ And he was right!” 

	Bardem also joked that for “many years” until his mother passed away in 2021, he wondered “where is my salary” for his appearance. “Still today, I don’t know what she did with my money.”

	Alongside his screen talk, Bardem has two films at the London Film Festival, which runs until Oct. 17, including Florian Zeller’s “Bunker” alongside his wife Penelope Cruz and Esteban Martinez’ “The Beloved.”

schema.headline: Javier Bardem on Adding Homoeroticism to 007 and Telling Sam Mendes That His ‘Skyfall’ Villain Should Be Someone Who ‘Wants to Have Sex With Bond’

title: Box Office: ‘The Social Reckoning’ Flops With $5.5 Million Debut, ‘Other Mommy’ Tops Box Office With $27.5 Million
description: “Other Mommy,” a horror movie starring Jessica Chastain as a double-jointed doppelgänger from hell, scared up $27.5 million in its box office debut.
body:
“Other Mommy,” a horror movie starring Jessica Chastain as a double-jointed doppelgänger from hell, scared up $27.5 million in its box office debut. Those ticket sales were enough to lead in North America over this weekend’s other new release, “The Social Reckoning,” which crumbled in fifth place with $5.5 million.

	“Other Mommy” landed above expectations despite being one of the worst-reviewed movies of the year. Universal and Blumhouse’s campy thriller, about a sinister paranormal entity who takes on the appearance of a young girl’s mother, was saddled with a 19% on Rotten Tomatoes and a tragic “D+” grade on CinemaScore exit polls. (Even last weekend’s bomb “Digger” managed to earn a “C+” grade on exit polls.) Those marks don’t bode well for box office longevity, though “Other Mommy” is well-positioned financially against a modest $18 million budget. The movie collected $17.69 million at the international box office, bringing its global tally to $45.19 million.
	

	“Horror movies are generally immune to a negative reception, but this is extreme,” says analyst David A. Gross, who publishes the box office newsletter FranchiseRe. “Business is going to drop sharply.” 


	“The Social Reckoning,” too, will have to combat poor word-of-mouth in the coming weeks. That’s a problem because Sony’s Facebook drama didn’t incentivize crowds in the first place. The R-rated movie, written and directed by Aaron Sorkin, was projected to open to $7 million to $8 million. Even those returns wouldn’t have come close to 2010’s “The Social Network,” which opened almost exactly 16 years ago to $22 million, not adjusted for inflation. Overseas, “The Social Reckoning” flatlined with $3.5 million from 29 markets for a $9 million worldwide start. 
	

	Critics and audiences were mixed on “The Social Reckoning,” which holds a 54% on Rotten Tomatoes and tepid “B-” grade on CinemaScore. The movie, picking up years after the first, follows a Facebook engineer (Mikey Madison) who leaks thousands of internal documents to a reporter (Jeremy Allen White) to blow the whistle on the company’s dark practices. Ticket buyers were mostly older males, a demographic that’s been slow to return to theaters since the pandemic.

	Comparisons between the two films were always going to be tough because “The Social Network” is widely considered one of the best films of the 2010s. That film, directed by David Fincher, written by Sorkin and starring Jessie Eisenberg as Zuckerberg, ended up earning $224 million globally and won four Oscars (including one for Sorkin’s screenplay). Because of the first film’s pedigree, and the fact that Fincher and Eisenberg didn’t return for the second, Sony tried to distance the association between the movies and called the follow-up a “companion piece” rather than a sequel. That’s also likely why the studio economized on the budget; “The Social Reckoning” carries a $30 million price tag while “The Social Network” cost $40 million.

	“Stories about corporate intrigue, money and power have found a home on TV. They lack the cinematic qualities that excite big-screen audiences,” Gross says. “The production cost was reasonable. But it’s still a lot of money to recoup at these box office levels.”

	Meanwhile, “Digger” cratered in its second weekend with $3.2 million from 3,321 theaters, a 60% decline from its dismal $8 million debut. So far, the Tom Cruise satire has limped to $14 million domestically and $35.3 million globally. Warner Bros. spent above $160 million to produce the film, which is shaping up to be one of the biggest bombs ever, with losses that could top $200 million theatrically. Given the scale of the disaster, Hollywood stars have been coming to the defense of “Digger,” with bold-faced names like Anne Hathaway, Jane Fonda, Guillermo del Toro and Mandy Patinkin praising the film and encouraging audiences to go to theaters. (Spoiler alert: It hasn’t worked.)

	Elsewhere, holdovers including Amazon MGM’s Colleen Hoover adaptation “Verity,” Sony’s “Resident Evil” reboot and Paramount’s Brad Pitt-led “Heart of the Beast” rounded out the box office charts.
	

	Second place went to “Verity” with $11.4 million from 3,572 theaters, a steep 64% decline from its opening weekend. The psychological thriller, starring Anne Hathaway and Dakota Johnson, is a win for Amazon MGM, having grossed $53 million in North America and $113 million worldwide to date against a $40 million budget.

	“Resident Evil” dropped to third place with $8.3 million in its fourth weekend. So far, the R-rated video game remake has generated a strong $138.5 million domestically and $300 million globally against a $75 million budget. This film and “Spider-Man: Brand New Day,” which is now the third-highest-grossing movie in history, will cushion any losses that Sony faces on “The Social Reckoning.”

	“Heart of the Beast,” a wilderness thriller about a man who survives a plane crash with his dog, was No. 4 with $7.1 million from 3,365 theaters in its third frame. The film has earned $49.6 million in North America and $131.3 million worldwide. It’s held steady but will need to keep chugging along in theaters to justify its $82 million production budget.

	Chris Rock’s directorial effort “Misty Green,” Alex Gibney’s probing Elon Musk documentary “Musk” and Neon’s Palme d’Or winning “Fjord” were among the new releases at the specialty box office. The commercial appeal of all three movies, which hope to find themselves in the Oscar race, will be tested as they roll out nationwide in the coming weeks.

	“Fjord,” a legal thriller about parents (Sebastian Stan and Renate Reinsve) who are suspected of child abuse, enjoyed the strongest start with $124,000 from just four theaters in New York and Los Angeles — translating to $31,00 per location.

	A24’s “Misty Green,” a showbiz drama about an actress (Rosalind Eleazar) fighting for her second act in Hollywood, collected $85,716 from six screens over the weekend — amounting to $14,286 per location — and $98,720 through its first four days in theaters.

	Bleecker Street’s “Musk,” an incisive look at the world’s richest man, generated $68,900 from four locations — averaging $17,225 per screen — over the weekend. Those returns are notable considering “Musk” runs at nearly four hours (and has an intermission!), which limits each theater’s daily showtimes.

	So far, October has been sluggish after a stronger-than-expected September at the box office. Revenues for the month are 23% ahead of the same point in 2025, which wound up as the lowest-grossing October in three decades, and 8% behind 2019, the last year before COVID upended the box office. So upcoming releases like Paramount’s video game adaptation “Street Fighter,” Disney’s survival thriller “Whalefall” and Warner Bros. and DC’s comic book-inspired “Clayface” are hoping to jolt attendance during the spookiest month of the year. 
	

	Although October might not be one for the record books, Hollywood has plenty to celebrate. Domestic revenues already eclipsed $8 billion —  a milestone the industry didn’t cross last year until December. With major blockbusters like “Avengers: Doomsday” and “Dune: Part III” on schedule, this year will easily be the biggest at the box office in post-pandemic times.

schema.headline: Box Office: ‘The Social Reckoning’ Flops With $5.5 Million Debut, ‘Other Mommy’ Tops Box Office With $27.5 Million

title: Disney Broadens Super Bowl LXI Plans With Pat McAfee, Next-Gen Stats
description:
Pat McAfee has been turning up in more places on ESPN. Add Super Bowl Sunday to the list.

	McAfee will lead a growing number of so-called “alterna-
body:
Pat McAfee has been turning up in more places on ESPN. Add Super Bowl Sunday to the list.

	McAfee will lead a growing number of so-called “alterna-casts” built around Disney’s 2027 Super Bowl plans. The outspoken host has been tapped to anchor “Field Pass,” a commentary-driven option that will play alongside a traditional broadcast of the Big Game on ABC and ESPN, and a Super Bowl version of the popular “ManningCast” featuring Peyton and Eli Manning, on ESPN2.
	

	Additionally, the company will offer a statistics-focused Super Bowl telecast, “Playbook,” which will be led by a team to be announced later.


	“Field Pass” will appear on ESPNU, while “Playbook” will run on the NFL Network on Super Bowl Sunday.

	The new options mean that Disney will, across its properties, offer five different Super Bowl telecasts. ESPN Deportes will feature a Spanish-language version of the gridiron classic. A Super Bowl “mega cast” has been in consideration at the company since 2021, when Disney struck a new rights deal with the NFL that will keep “Monday Night Football” on the air at ESPN through 2033. Since that time, the league and the company have become even closer, with the league taking a 10% stake in ESPN as part of a deal that put NFL Network and NFL RedZone under the ESPN umbrella.

	Many media companies have been experimenting with bespoke telecasts aimed at a narrower niche of viewers, like young women or sports-stats aficionados. In 2020,  Disney devised a range of bespoke telecasts of a Wild Card game, one tailored for younger viewers on the company’s Freeform cable outlet. It has created “viewing party” sessions that rely on sports celebrities and others that work to appeal those interested in sports wagering. In 2019, ESPN aired a version of the NFL Draft tailored for sports aficionados, while ABC ran one aimed at general audiences that featured music and was hosted in part by “Good Morning Anchor” Robin Roberts. The company has also tried its hand at “mega-casting” a handful of “Monday Night Football” games on ESPN, ESPN2 and ABC, and tapped characters from Marvel, Pixar and the Disney Channel for kids-and-families versions of games.
	

	Fans won’t have to wait until 2027 to start trying out some of the new concepts. Both of the new alterna-casts will air tied to “Monday Night Football” during select weeks. McAfee’s “Field Pass”  will air on ESPN2 during five weeks of the regular season and will start in the current season’s sixth week. “Playbook” will start in the fifth week and air seven different Monday telecasts. Field Yates, Chase Daniel, Louis Riddick and Seth Walder will lead the telecasts on a rotating basis.

schema.headline: Disney Broadens Super Bowl LXI Plans With Pat McAfee, Next-Gen Stats

title: Christopher Nolan’s ‘The Odyssey’ Overtakes ‘Avatar: The Way of Water’ as Korea’s Biggest International Film of All Time (EXCLUSIVE)
description: Christopher Nolan’s “The Odyssey” has overtaken “Avatar: The Way of Water” in local-currency terms to become the highest-grossing international rele
body:
Christopher Nolan’s “The Odyssey” has overtaken “Avatar: The Way of Water” in local-currency terms to become the highest-grossing international release in Korean box office history, with a cumulative KRW139.2 billion ($101.5 million) as of Oct. 11.

	The Universal release now ranks as the top Hollywood title ever in the territory. Only two Korean films have earned more. Jang Hang-jun’s “The King’s Warden” took the all-time record this year with KRW153.2 billion ($111.7 million), while Lee Byeong-heon’s 2019 comedy “Extreme Job” sits just ahead of “The Odyssey” on KRW139.6 billion ($101.8 million).
	

	Admissions for “The Odyssey” stand at 12 million, equivalent to about 24% of the country’s population. No other international film has passed 10 million admissions this year. “The Odyssey” also held the No. 1 spot for seven straight weekends, the longest such streak for an international title in Korea.


	It is now Nolan’s biggest film in Korea, as well as the biggest Universal title there. It holds the Imax record too, a total that continues to grow as the film plays into its 10th week on the format’s screens. No film released in Korea has drawn more admissions on Imax and Dolby Cinema screens, and Imax shows sold out continuously through the fifth week of release, the longest run of sellouts on record.

	The film crossed 10 million admissions in 33 days, faster than any non-franchise international title. It was the first international film carrying a 15+ rating to reach that level, and the first August release of any kind to do so. The result makes Nolan the first director with two non-franchise international films above 10 million admissions in Korea.
	

	Demand built well before opening. “The Odyssey” posted the year’s highest advance ticket sales and led Korean presales for 43 consecutive days through Sept. 14, the longest such run this year. As of Sept. 13, it had been the top international film at the box office for 40 days in a row, also a record.

	The Korean promotional tour set several post-pandemic marks. A Seoul press conference drew 209 members of the media, the biggest turnout for such a tour since the pandemic. A premiere event hosted by CGV attracted 32,411 applications, a 463-to-1 ratio and the highest participation the exhibitor has recorded for a Korea premiere. The visiting delegation made 11 appearances across Korean TV programs and online content, and the tour’s Cine21 Master Talk passed 1 million views, the most in the series’ history.

	Jungkook of BTS, TXT’s Soobin and members of Riize were among the Korean stars who recommended the film of their own accord, fueling conversation on social media. Content created voluntarily by influencers and YouTubers generated an estimated KRW1.27 billion (about $1 million) in earned media value, while sales of books linked to “The Odyssey” rose 30-fold after release.

	Nolan also became the first international film director to appear on Korea’s non-drama buzzworthiness chart, a ranking usually filled by local television personalities and entertainers. Each new batch of Imax tickets brought congestion on CGV’s servers, followed by fresh sellouts.

schema.headline: Christopher Nolan’s ‘The Odyssey’ Overtakes ‘Avatar: The Way of Water’ as Korea’s Biggest International Film of All Time (EXCLUSIVE)

title: AI-Native Studios Can Create Original IP While Traditional Studios Keep Their Edge, VFX Veteran Hong Jae Cheol Says at Busan
description: Small, AI-native companies running automated pipelines can develop their own intellectual property, while traditional studios hold on to their advan
body:
Small, AI-native companies running automated pipelines can develop their own intellectual property, while traditional studios hold on to their advantages in established franchises, production infrastructure, talent and distribution, according to VFX veteran Hong Jae Cheol.

	Hong, a producer-director at Viscode who began his career at Industrial Light & Magic and worked on films including “Iron Man,” “Transformers” and “Pirates of the Caribbean,” laid out that vision at the InnoAsia AI Creators Camp, held Sunday at the Busan International Film Festival‘s Asian Contents & Film Market in Busan. “We are moving from using AI to generate individual images toward using AI as part of a complete production workflow,” he said.
	

	AI is changing the production model, Hong argued, while traditional visual effects remain essential to making generated material usable on screen. He framed the future as a hybrid, and a partnership between AI and human creativity, rather than a wholesale replacement of existing studios.


	Hong contrasted a conventional live-action and VFX process, involving 3D assets, animation, rendering and compositing, with an AI-assisted approach. In the latter, actors perform on a controlled set; AI generates environments and visual elements; and VFX artists handle tracking, integration and finishing. He also outlined current AI applications across VFX, animation and filmmaking, including rotoscoping, cleanup, previs, character design, camera tests and environment creation.

	Mark Wachholz, chief creative director of Berlin-based Dreamkite Studios, whose AI films “The Cinema That Never Was” and “Céremony” have won top prizes at AI film festivals, approached the shift from the creative side. He described AI co-creation as an invitation to give up some control and allow for surprise, framing the process as “exploring instead of controlling” and “finding instead of knowing.” He also argued that new tools require new ways of thinking, rather than simply applying old methods to new technology.
	

	Director Ahn Jaehong of Climax Studio, who turned to AI filmmaking after arm injuries ended his work behind the camera, brought the discussion back to directing and production. He mapped a workflow from prompts and camera information to scene context, shot lists, storyboards, character and prop sheets, locations and keyframes. The sequence reinforced a point shared by the speakers: AI can assist across multiple stages, but filmmakers still need to shape the story, visual design and final result.

	Hong summed up the distinction: “AI is just a tool; film is a sequence.” The discussion centered on how that tool might become part of a connected filmmaking process, with human direction and VFX expertise still determining how its images fit together.

schema.headline: AI-Native Studios Can Create Original IP While Traditional Studios Keep Their Edge, VFX Veteran Hong Jae Cheol Says at Busan

title: ‘12.12: The Day’ Director Kim Sung-soo Says AI ‘Shows What’s in Your Imagination’
description: Kim Sung-soo, director of Korean box office hit “12.12: The Day,” once saw AI as a destroyer of the film industry. Speaking Sunday at a session host
body:
Kim Sung-soo, director of Korean box office hit “12.12: The Day,” once saw AI as a destroyer of the film industry. Speaking Sunday at a session hosted by Kling AI at the Busan International Film Festival‘s Asian Contents & Film Market, he described how it has instead become part of his craft.

	His turning point was “Worm Train,” an eight-minute short he first gave up on because AI couldn’t render its key scene, a giant insect colliding with a packed train crowd. Months later, the technology had caught up. “Technology doesn’t replace creativity. It shows what’s in your imagination,” Kim said. The project changed how he imagines and collaborates, he added: “I’ll never go back to the way I used to make films.”
	

	He did not make it alone. Kim assembled a nine-person team, including an animation art director and a music director. Though the short could have been made entirely with AI, he said, they chose to generate only part of it and handle the rest with conventional filmmaking methods. He plans a similar hybrid approach for a seven-part drama series he is developing. Its nearly 15-minute opening chase on the Gyeongin Expressway, which he said would require “enormous financial resources” to shoot conventionally, will first be generated with AI, then used to decide which shots need actors on set and where traditional VFX come in.


	Kim was joined by Harry Hyun, director and CEO of AI production company MooAm; Chinese animation director Li Wei, co-director of “Jiang Ziya”; and Lee Sangwook, producer and team manager at MBC C&I’s AI Contents Lab.
	

	Li made a similar case for animation. Presenting a trailer for “Born of the Tide,” a 105-minute AI-animated feature about China’s boat-dwelling Tanka community, he said the technology works best at the trial-and-error stage: concept designs that once took enormous time to draw by hand can now be visualized quickly and shared with the team. “AI can generate many things, but the choice and the details all come down to the director,” he said.

	Hyun agreed that filmmaking skill is what makes the difference. “Faces look identical, sets look identical, lighting looks identical,” she said of AI output made without it. That is why MooAm looks for AI artists who have directed at least one live-action short.

	Otherwise, she said, AI production is not fundamentally different from a conventional shoot, only more efficient. What changes is the crew. Her directing team now includes an “AI coordinator,” who decides which cuts will be generated, keeps a continuity script for them and checks with AI artists that everything cuts together. Even assistant directors need a basic grasp of AI, as gray screens marked with tracking points replace green screens.

	Building those skills is also a priority for Lee, whose lab is producing “Rendering Love,” a short-form K-pop romantic comedy about a virtual idol group, with “Parasite” producer Barunson E&A developing the story. “If even one or two individuals lag on the learning curve, overall quality can suffer,” he said of keeping pace as models update.

	Mastering the tools won’t settle every question, though. Kim argued that rules on commercial use and permissions should be settled before the industry sets any technical standards. “Whenever I generate outputs, I scrutinize the results closely to ensure they do not infringe upon existing works or violate anyone’s publicity rights,” he said.

	“In the future, we won’t call AI movies ‘AI movies,’ just as we no longer call films ‘color movies,’” Kim said.

schema.headline: ‘12.12: The Day’ Director Kim Sung-soo Says AI ‘Shows What’s in Your Imagination’

title: ‘Wildwood’ Review: Laika’s Most Ambitious Feature to Date Is a Richly Textured, Transportive Fairytale Epic
description: “Enjoy handmade art before it’s gone forever.” Keen-eyed viewers may read these words fleetingly on screen in the early stages of “Wildwood,” amid a
body:
“Enjoy handmade art before it’s gone forever.” Keen-eyed viewers may read these words fleetingly on screen in the early stages of “Wildwood,” amid a wealth of fast-passing sights and sight gags as its young heroine cycles furiously through the homey, bustling streets of Portland, Oregon. Printed on a sign next to the craggly wares of a local ceramicist, the line gently pokes fun at the city’s wholesome, hippy-dippy spirit — but it’s also a sincere advertisement for the predominantly handcrafted virtues of “Wildwood” itself. If the in-joke sounds a little self-congratulatory, director Travis Knight and his team have a right to brag: The sixth feature from independent animation studio Laika is a stunner, a lovingly tactile and thumbprinted feat of stop-motion artistry on a scale rarely seen in the medium, that stands out by a mile in a cartoon marketplace ruled by sheeny, uncanny digital graphics. 
	

	That’s not in itself a revelation. Laika’s pleasingly organic, idiosyncratic (and let it be said, subtly CG-augmented) visual style has impressed from their 2009 debut, Henry Selick’s modern children’s classic “Coraline,” through to the likably goofy comedy “Missing Link” a decade later. Both those films opted for a cozily oddball storytelling style that matched the intimacy of their craftsmanship. In 2016’s historical Japanese adventure “Kubo and the Two Strings,” however, Knight pushed this decidedly miniaturist medium into brashly epic territory — an objective he pursues even more ambitiously in this sprawling 130-minute adventure, which narratively runs the gamut from gothic fairytale to visceral fantasy warfare. Some longtime Laika fans may harbor warmer feelings for the studio’s smaller, quirkier outings, but as both a formal achievement and a generation-crossing crowdpleaser, “Wildwood” is a spectacular success. 
	

	If the film is, at a story level, somewhat more generic than we’ve come to expect from the Laika playbook, that also goes for the book it’s adapted from. A 500-page-plus doorstop by indie musician Colin Meloy (of the Decemberists fame) that straddles the border between children’s and YA literature, the novel shows no great originality of prose or concept — fragments of works by C.S. Lewis, J.R.R. Tolkien, Enid Blyton and Kenneth Grahame are all mixed into its narrative and imagery, not to mention a sizable chunk of Jim Henson’s film “Labyrinth” — but it’s an absorbing yarn nonetheless. The same goes for the film, in which the studio’s regular screenwriter Chris Butler perhaps even improves on the source material: The dialogue is sparky, the relationships quick-drawn but genuinely felt. 

	It opens on a sequence of quite frightening, disorienting strangeness that immediately makes sense of the film’s outwardly surprising PG-13 certificate — presaging a degree of bloodshed and emotional intensity not to be ignored by parents seeking an animated film to babysit their little ones. As a thunderstorm rages outside, a young boy in an imposing woodland castle steps onto a high terrace outside his bedroom, and deliberately plunges to his death before his distraught mother can stop him; as crowds gather at the site of the tragedy, it’s discovered that the boy was merely an android, his chest shattered to reveal the metal cogs within.

	It’s some time before we’re given the context for this solemn, cryptically beautiful opening gambit, as we cut to an altogether more recognizable childhood: that of precocious 12-year-old Prue (voiced by Peyton Elizabeth Lee), who lives with her bohemian hipster parents (Jake Johnson and Maya Erskine) and baby brother Mac in a tranquil Portland suburb, and who’s just beginning to wish for a life less ordinary, or at least less oatmealy. Her parents are earnest, overprotective types (Mac is never allowed outside, for reasons initially unknown) who subscribe to much regional lore and superstition, particularly regarding the so-called Impassable Wilderness on the edge of town — a temptingly dense forest that locals are forbidden to enter.

	Enter it we shall, of course, but only under dire circumstances — when Prue, skeptically ignoring her parents’ instructions when asked to look after Mac for an afternoon, takes him to a local playground, only to watch helplessly as the infant is lifted up, up and away by a distinctly Hitchcockian (and quite possibly literal) murder of crows. Cue an enthralling chase sequence, doubling back through those higgledy-piggledy Portland streetscapes, toward the woods — the impenetrable thickets and thorns of which magically part in her presence. (Another point of mystery to be bookmarked for later.)
	

	She’s initially joined in her panicked search by well-meaning but hopelessly nerdy classmate Curtis (Jacob Tremblay) — who, of course, turns out to be made of sterner stuff than you might think — but they’re soon separated in a dizzyingly diverse and surreal ecosystem in which separate patches of land are variously ruled by Redcoat-styled military coyotes, highly intelligent and supersized birds of prey, and human figures ranging from kindly sorceresses to hulking bandits to petty bureaucrats. Prue soon finds her already daunting search complicated by long-festering tensions between these factions, with the powerfully villainous and violently broken-hearted Dowager Governess (superbly voiced by Carey Mulligan) at the crux of them all. The outsider girl’s innocent invasion may just be the thing that finally triggers a war.

	It’s a saga at once complex and classically simple, rife with timeworn fairytale tropes from grieving queens to imperilled babes in the wood, and stuffed with enough peppy secondary characters to justify an all-star voice ensemble. (Mahershala Ali is a gruff but gold-hearted warrior; Awkwafina a snide but helpful rat heavily indebted to E.B. White’s Templeton.) It runs into a lull here and there — the runtime, while swaggeringly impressive, is not altogether necessary — but it’s largely entrancing, not least because each newly revealed nook of these infinite wilds gives a crack team of claymation artists new tones, textures, creatures and mythological reference points to play with. 

	A majestic, outsize golden eagle (voiced, naturally, with regal authority by Angela Bassett) who comes to Prue’s rescue at one vital point is a thing of immense wonder, its every feather as painstakingly articulated as the swarming ivy leaves strangling certain sectors of the forest; a towering holy tree moves ravishingly through several seasons of foliage in a matter of seconds. But the animators are no less attentive to fine-grained details: the characterful snarling set of each coyote’s jaw, or a tear glistening in close-up on a soft, reddened cheek. It’s all exquisitely lit, moreover, by veteran DP Caleb Deschanel (“The Black Stallion,” “The Passion of the Christ”), whether lending just the right crepuscular glow to an enchanted glade, or manipulating the spindly shadows of the woods at witching hour.
	

	Dario Marianelli’s score is likewise restless and many-hued, alternately taking inspiration from whirling Celtic strings, military-tattoo percussion and jaunty acoustic instrumentation — though an early needle-drop of Loretta Lynn’s country-rock banger “Portland Oregon” is never matched for its unexpected modernity. (Meloy’s band contributes a pleasantly inspirational closing-credits ditty.) “Wildwood” is on the verge of visual and sonic overkill, but abundance is very much the point of a story about exploring and embracing all corners of the world around you, even those you’ve been explicitly told to stay away from. In that spirit, too, Knight’s film borrows much from the library of fantasy and folklore, but with enough of its own exuberance and imagination to feel like a new standard. Perhaps handmade art isn’t going anywhere just yet.

Patrick Clancy, Rachel Danis
                          All Aboard the Chicago Marathon Train
                          ... Baby Bump on Display!!!
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              October 11, 2026
                            8:20 AM PDT
                                                                      |
                                                                Updated 
                                  October 11, 2026
                                9:42 AM PDT
                                    
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Patrick Clancy and his pregnant wife, Rachel Danis, are taking in the Windy City ... hopping aboard Chicago's 'L' train Saturday, seemingly in town for the annual marathon.
      
    
            TMZ obtained photos of Patrick and Rachel boarding the elevated train on October 10, with Rachel's baby bump visible ... amid the couple's recent pregnancy announcement.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Patrick, meanwhile, was carrying a bag labeled "Chicago Marathon" ... suggesting the couple may be in town for Sunday's big race, although it's unclear whether just one or both plan on participating.
      

                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            As we previously reported, Patrick and Rachel confirmed they're expecting a child together during an emotional sit-down with "60 Minutes" last month. The news marked a major new chapter for Patrick, who lost his three children -- Cora, Dawson and Callan -- in January 2023.
      
    
            Patrick's former wife, Lindsay Clancy, was charged in connection with the children's deaths. Her murder trial ended in a mistrial in September after jurors were unable to reach a unanimous verdict due to a holdout juror going against the pack's decision.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Patrick and Rachel married in April and spoke publicly together for the first time during the "60 Minutes" interview ... discussing their relationship, the public scrutiny they've faced and their plans to build a family.
      
    
            Patrick also spoke about wanting to tell his future children about their late siblings, making clear that moving forward doesn't mean leaving their memories behind.
      
    
            The couple's Chicago outing comes as they prepare for the arrival of their baby ... with the two seemingly navigating the city like any other pair enjoying a weekend away.

title: Cornell University Cancels Homecoming Concert Amid Alleged Gang Rape Fallout
description:
Cornell University
                          Homecoming Concert Cancelled
                          St
body:
Cornell University
                          Homecoming Concert Cancelled
                          Students Stand By Jane Doe
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              October 11, 2026
                            9:07 AM PDT
                                                                            
              
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Cornell University’s homecoming concert has been canceled amid the school's sexual assault scandal, as students rally in support of the alleged victim, identified as Jane Doe.
      
    
            The Cornell Concerts Commission announced it's pulling the plug on its planned Homecoming Concert featuring indie-pop duo Between Friends, which had been scheduled for October 17 at Barton Hall.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            The student-run group says the decision comes as it calls on Cornell's administration to do more to support survivors of sexual violence ... saying in a statement to social media, "The Cornell Concert Commission is a student-run organization and, as students, we stand with Jane Doe and all survivors of sexual violence."
      

            The cancellation comes as Cornell faces mounting backlash over its handling of allegations stemming from an alleged 2024 gang rape at the university's Chi Phi fraternity house.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            As TMZ previously reported, we obtained text messages that offer additional insight into the case and the allegations that have rocked the university.
      
    
            In a text chain between one of the accused students Jonathan Newell and Jane Doe days after the alleged incident, Jonathan apologizes to Jane and says, "You're an amazing person and I genuinely hope ur not catching as much heat from this as we r. We've been shutting down any stories we've heard but again I'm so so sorry."
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            In another thread we obtained, accused former frat member Matthew Ingalls consoles Jane after she mentions having a UTI, and says of the rumors, "Stupid bitches like to yap, and the fact they're doing it shows that they're jealous of you for any number of reasons."
      
    
            The commission apologized to students who had planned to attend, saying Between Friends hopes to connect with local fans at a later date. It says it plans to organize a charity concert featuring local performers, including student bands and DJs, with all proceeds going to the Rape, Abuse & Incest National Network.
      
    
            The investigation into Jane Doe's case has been recently reopened by the Tompkins District Attorney.

schema.headline: Cornell University Cancels Homecoming Concert Amid Alleged Gang Rape Fallout
